extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students or general readers studying American government and Congress
extracted.subtask_short: explaining US Congress structure and rules
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing the composition, powers, procedures, privileges, election methods, and constitutional limits of the U.S. House and Senate, with historical examples and critiques. Covers districting, terms, nominations, contested elections, privileges, quorum and session rules, and the Seventeenth Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Districting should be compact and contiguous / anti-gerrymandering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An illustration of 'compact and contiguous territory.' The district system under the gerrymander has frequently resulted in the grossest misrepresentation of party strength in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and historical notes: "saddle bag" district in Illinois; Indiana 1892 gerrymander elected 11 Democrats with fewer votes than Republicans; 1894 national vote-to-seat disproportionality (Republicans 48.4% vote ⇒ 68.8% seats). Implicit standard: districts ideally compact and contiguous to avoid crowding opposition counties into single districts and to secure disproportionate seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: House member term length
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of the member of the House is two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms: short term with long delay before taking seat (often more than a year) diverts attention to campaigning, reduces capacity to gain experience, may leave defeated members disgruntled and open to pernicious influences; but long terms risk misrepresentation without recall/dissolution mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner of House elections (state prescription subject to Congressional override)
rubrics_metrics.description: The time, place, and manner of holding elections for Representatives may be prescribed by the state legislature subject to the provision that Congress may at any time by law make or alter such regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By laws of 1871 and 1872 Congress required ballot voting and uniform timing: Tuesday following the first Monday in November, with limited exceptions for some states to hold earlier elections according to custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination methods for House candidates (party machinery vs direct primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates are nominated by district conventions of delegates or, where primary legislation has been adopted, by an official direct primary election for each party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conventions remain, district conventions represent local units (counties, wards). Under direct-primary laws, a candidate's name is put on the primary ballot by petition and party voters select the nominee. Representatives-at-large are nominated by state conventions or state primaries. Examples of states adopting primaries are listed (e.g., Wisconsin, Nebraska, Oregon, Kansas, Oklahoma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contested election procedures in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: The House is judge of the election, returns, and qualifications of its own members; the law requires notice to the member whose seat is contested and specification of grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: contestant serves notice and specifies grounds; the member answers; papers transmitted to House; clerk compiles records; Speaker refers to one of the three House committees on elections; testimony taken; contestants heard and may be represented by counsel; committee reports to the House which usually accepts it. Political reality: committees often have majority from dominant party, so contested elections may be decided in party interest unless blatantly obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: House and Senate committees on elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The House has three committees on elections and the Senate has one committee on elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These committees investigate election contests and perform functions akin to a court of law in adjudicating contested seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate equal representation rule (two Senators per state)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution prescribes that there shall be two Senators from each state; no state, without its consent, shall be deprived of equal representation in the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect: absolute equality leads to disproportionate representation relative to population (examples comparing eastern and western states circa 1900). The text critiques this as violating democratic principle of representation by population, though in practice Senators of small and large states do not necessarily align exclusively by state-size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of Senators (constitutional)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Senator must be not less than thirty years old, an inhabitant of the state for which he is elected, and a United States citizen of nine years' standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional limits: neither the Senate, Congress, nor a state can add to these qualifications. The Senate's judgment power is to determine whether members possess the constitutionally prescribed qualifications; it may expel a member for disorderly behavior that lowers the body's standard or brings it into disrepute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate power cannot add qualifications to members beyond Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate, under its power to judge of the qualifications of its members, cannot add any qualifications fixed in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: debate over excluding Senator Reed Smoot (polygamist) — argument that Senate should not add new qualifications but only determine whether constitutional qualifications are met; Senate retains expulsion power for misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical method of electing Senators by state legislatures (pre-1913) and its procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously Senators were elected by state legislatures; the legislature (immediately preceding expiration) was to elect the Senator by separate viva voce votes in each house, and if no majority then met in joint assembly and voted until a Senator was elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice party caucus selection predominated; deadlocks were frequent (examples: Pennsylvania 1899; Delaware contest involving J. E. Addicks 1895–1903). Criticisms: use of money, deadlocks, and alleged plutocratic influence spurred movement for direct election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth Amendment provisions (popular election of Senators)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment provides that Senators shall be elected by the people for six years; electors in each state must have qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the state legislature; vacancies are to be filled by writs of election, with state legislatures empowered to allow temporary executive appointments until election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption history: by 1913 Congress passed the resolution and states ratified; effect: states must make provisions for nomination (primaries or conventions). If a state fails to provide for popular election, Congress may act under Article I, section 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination procedures under popular election of Senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Seventeenth Amendment it will be necessary for states to make provision for the nomination of candidates; states with direct primary laws applicable to Senators will likely continue them while remaining states may retain conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 1912 many states already used primaries for Senatorial nominations. The amendment left to states the method of nomination, though Congress retains power to legislate timing/manner if states fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senator term length and continuity (classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a Senator is six years; the Senate is a continuous body with one-third of members going out every two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At first session (1789) Senate divided by lot into three classes so terms expire in staggered fashion; in practice Senators are frequently reelected and long-serving Senators are common, often more so in smaller states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members' compensation determined by law and history of salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators and Representatives shall receive compensation for their services as ascertained by law and paid from the U.S. Treasury; historically per diem, later fixed salaries and allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History: per diem until 1855, $3000 in 1855, $5000 in 1865, $7500 in 1873 (repealed then restored later). 1907 salary fixed at $7500 plus allowance for clerk hire, stationery, and traveling expenses. Notes on campaign finance laws (corporations forbidden to contribute to federal campaigns in 1907; candidate expenditure disclosure laws 1910–11; spending limits indicated for candidates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege from arrest during attendance (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members enjoy freedom from arrest during attendance on sessions and in going to and returning from the same, except for treason, felony, and breach of the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This privilege exempts members from processes the disobedience of which would be punishable by imprisonment (e.g., jury duty, court testimony, civil suits) but 'breach of the peace' is construed broadly to include all indictable offenses; members thus have no exemption from ordinary criminal law. Reasonable delays and deviations when traveling to/from Congress allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech or Debate privilege (freedom of speech during debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any speech or debate no member of either house shall be questioned in any other place; members are protected from prosecution for libel or slander for anything said in Congress or in committees in the legitimate discharge of legislative duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates in English parliamentary practice; aimed to protect members from arbitrary arrest or liability to constituents. Members assume privilege includes right to circulate speeches nationwide; protects official publications and legitimate legislative acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-organization constitutional limits on each house
rubrics_metrics.description: Each house's internal organization is limited by certain Constitutional provisions: Vice-President presides over Senate; expulsion requires two-thirds vote; each house must keep and publish a journal (except secret parts); one-fifth of members present can demand a yeas-and-nays record by roll-call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject to these limits, houses can elect their own officers, compel attendance of members, and prescribe rules of procedure and discipline. Vice-President has no vote except tie in Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to compel witness attendance and punish contempt is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither house has a general power to punish outsiders for contempt; when examination of private citizens is necessary for legislative duties Congress may require attendance and compel testimony, but punishment is judicial in nature and limited to the session in which condemnation occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court holdings limit Congress's power to punish its members or private citizens to imprisonment during the remainder of that session; power to punish outsiders is not general but situational for legislative necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum requirement and ant-dilatory rule (Reed rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quorum necessary to do business is a majority of all members, though a smaller number may adjourn day-to-day and are authorized to compel attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minority tactics historically included refusing to answer roll-call to prevent a quorum and delay business. Speaker Reed (1890) held that members physically present but declining to answer should be counted present for quorum determination; House rule authorized the clerk to count as present those physically present but refusing to answer. Example of enforcement in Congressional Record: Sergeant-at-Arms bringing absentees, noting arrested members as present and discharged, roll-call procedure, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional sessions scheduling (annual sessions and two sessions per Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution requires an annual session of Congress, beginning the first Monday in December unless Congress by law appoints a different day; normally each Congress has two sessions (long session beginning in December of odd year and second session beginning in December of even year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: long session often adjourned spring/summer; second session ends March 4; each Congress expires at noon March 4 of odd year; result: new President inherits a new Congress at start of administration; lag between election and seating can allow outgoing (defeated) members to legislate, creating 'lame-duck' effects and opportunities for corporate influence during second session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special sessions called by the President
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may call special sessions of Congress to convene either house or both on extraordinary occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: July 4, 1861 call to prepare for Civil War; President Wilson convened Congress in April 1913 to revise the tariff. The Senate is often called at beginning of a new administration to confirm appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No constitutional provision for constituent instructions of members
rubrics_metrics.description: No provision is made in the Constitution whereby members of Congress can be instructed by their constituents; representatives are theoretically national legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice state legislatures sometimes instruct Senators and Representatives by resolutions, but there is no penalty for violating such instructions because a state legislature cannot compel resignation; members are politically sensitive to party/community leaders' wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancy filling for the House (special elections)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a vacancy occurs in the House by death, resignation, or otherwise, a special election is held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit procedural standard: vacancies are filled by popular special election; contrasted with Senate temporary appointments allowed by state legislature under Seventeenth Amendment provisions.
